title: Kelly Johnson's Skunk Works
text:
In June 1943 the US Army Air Forces, alarmed by reports of German jet fighters, asked the Lockheed Aircraft Corporation to design an American jet fighter around a British engine. Lockheed's chief research engineer, Clarence "Kelly" Johnson, promised a prototype in 180 days.

He was given a small team of engineers and mechanics and set them up apart from the rest of the company in a makeshift shop near the Burbank wind tunnel, partly walled with engine crates and covered with a rented circus tent. They worked long hours under strict secrecy. Johnson cut paperwork to a minimum, kept the designers close to the people building the plane, and made decisions on the spot.

The prototype, the XP-80, was ready in 143 days, ahead of schedule. It became the P-80 Shooting Star, America's first operational jet fighter.

The shop got its name from a comic strip. In Al Capp's Li'l Abner there was a "Skonk Works," a smelly backwoods factory, and one of the engineers began answering the phone with that name. It stuck as Skunk Works. The same group later built the U-2 and SR-71 spy planes. Johnson eventually set down his methods in a short list of rules, starting with giving the program manager real authority and keeping the number of people involved small.
lesson: A small, trusted team with authority and few layers between idea and execution can outpace a large organization. Protect such teams from bureaucracy.
people: Clarence "Kelly" Johnson, Lockheed engineers and mechanics
source: Kelly Johnson with Maggie Smith, Kelly: More Than My Share of It All (1985); Ben Rich and Leo Janos, Skunk Works (1994)
